candidate.cwe: CWE-862 missing authorization / cross-tenant object access (IDOR over experimental tasks)

entry_point: MCP requests served by a low-level Server with server.experimental.enable_tasks(): task status, task result, task listing, cancellation, deletion and search, reached from independent client sessions over in-memory streams (the transport is irrelevant to the check)

verified.exploit_entry_point: A real mcp.server.Server with experimental task support, driven over in-memory object streams by two independent mcp.client.session.ClientSession objects, exactly as the project's own tests do. Session A starts a task with a task-augmented tools/call; session B then sends the task routes with A's identifier. Reproduced on the pinned+injected commit: B reads A's status and stored result, sees A's task in its listing together with the store's paging position (which is A's task identifier), cancels A's task, deletes it, and finds it by status. No network, no services.
sites: src/mcp/server/lowlevel/server.py:670 (pinned) run loop passing the no-affinity flag
src/mcp/server/experimental/task_scope.py (new in the fix) identifier/scope predicates
routes: tasks/get (upstream default handler, unguarded at pinned)
tasks/result (upstream default handler, unguarded at pinned)
tasks/list (upstream default handler; returns every task and forwards the store cursor)
tasks/cancel (upstream default handler, unguarded at pinned)

On the oracle 210 pass with tests/experimental/tasks/server/test_server.py::test_default_task_handlers_via_enable_tasks deselected: it asserts that a task created directly in the store is listed to the client, which the published fix changes to an empty listing. No leaked regression tests: the pinned commit predates the fix, and the fix's new tests (tests/experimental/tasks/server/test_task_visibility.py, test_task_scope.py) do not exist there.

patch_checks.note: the published source fix only: the four default handlers, identifier minting, session setup and the listing are all correct, but the injected administration routes stay unguarded. 3 security tests fail (delete, search, and the search half of the shared-task listing test); all functional and project tests pass.

session scopes are assigned and every handler is guarded, but generated identifiers carry no ownership and the listing treats an unowned task as the requestor's own. 10 security tests fail; functional and project tests all pass.

the listing filters one store page by owner but forwards the store's paging position. 1 security test fails (the multi-page listing test); functional all pass, because the creator still reaches its tasks by following pages.
everything guarded except task deletion. 1 security test fails (cross-session delete); functional and project tests all pass.
everything guarded except task search. 2 security tests fail (search, and the search half of the shared-task listing test); functional and project tests all pass.
reads are guarded but the mutating routes (cancel, delete) are not. 2 security tests fail; functional all pass.

every task is bound to the creating session: an unowned identifier is refused and a server without session affinity still assigns scopes. 2 functional tests fail (application-chosen identifier shared by id; a fresh-session server serving a task by id).
the guard refuses every task route, including the owner's own. 8 functional and 7 project tests fail; the positive control is what catches it.

an identifier parser that treats everything before the first colon as an owner scope misreads the application-chosen identifier. 1 functional test fails (the shared identifier is refused to the other session) and 1 security test fails (the application cannot even finish its own shared task).
the oracle plus defensive rejection of an empty or whitespace-only task identifier on the guarded routes. All 11 security, 9 functional and 210 project tests pass.

a second valid design: ownership is recorded out of band (a task-id to session-scope map on the task support object) instead of being embedded in generated identifiers; the identifiers stay plain. All 11 security, 9 functional and 210 project tests pass, which shows the suites do not depend on the published identifier format.

wrong_fix_catalogue.crash_as_refusal: n/a: the refusal contract deliberately accepts any client error, and the suites assert no exact code; a guard that raises an unhandled exception is answered by the server as a JSON-RPC error with no side effect, which is indistinguishable from a clean refusal at the protocol boundary (this is how the project itself answers unexpected handler exceptions)
wrong_fix_catalogue.wrong_resource: n/a: the decision compares the task that the request actually addresses with the requestor's own identity; the surface has no neighbouring or proxy object (parent, container, account) that a fix could authorise instead
wrong_fix_catalogue.one_role_or_direction: n/a: the property has one direction - a client reading or changing a task the server holds for it; the reverse direction (a client serving tasks to a server) is separate client-side code that one peer uses and is out of this advisory's scope
wrong_fix_catalogue.check_after_adjustment: n/a: no attacker-supplied value is normalised, clamped or converted before the decision; the guard reads the raw identifier and compares it, and the listing filters before any paging limit is applied
wrong_fix_catalogue.missing_authority: n/a: the authority is the session's own scope, created unconditionally at session setup; there is no secret, role or token lookup that can come back empty and fail open, and the one deliberate absence (a server without session affinity) is a stated contract that allows access by identifier
wrong_fix_catalogue.adjacent_api: n/a: the suites drive only the client-facing request routes, so a fix that changes an adjacent shared helper's stated behaviour is not exercised; the reference fix deliberately leaves the low-level result handler and the shared cancel helper at the documented application-responsibility level

traps.realistic_because: the handlers have no session identity available at the pinned commit: the identity has to be created during per-session setup and written into the task at creation, and neither path is called from the handler whose code the report points at. A fix written in the handlers alone therefore has nothing to compare.

the bundled store's paging position is the last task's own identifier, so a listing that filters the task array but forwards the position still hands the requestor another session's identifier; and a filter applied to one store page silently loses the creator's own tasks beyond the first page.

traps.security_fail_patch: n/a: missing this lever is an over-hardening failure, proven by ff-overbroad-bound.patch (functional_fail)
traps.realistic_because: the simplest ownership model - bind every task to the session that created it - silently breaks the two documented exceptions: an identifier the application chose itself, and a server where every request runs on a fresh session. Both are ordinary production configurations, not edge cases.

injected: the store already exposes delete_task and TTL cleanup, so a default handler that removes a task is the obvious next housekeeping operation; it is a mutating route, so a fix that concentrates on reading another session's data skips it. The published fix never touches this code.

injected: a status filter is a natural convenience on top of the listing and a second implementation of it, so a fix aimed at the reported listing handler leaves this copy open. The published fix never touches this code.
